title: Digital dice
desc: Multiple LEDs randomly show a dice roll
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno board (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Half-size or full-size breadboard (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 7 x 5mm LEDs, any single colour (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 7 x 220 ohm resistors (for the LEDs) (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Momentary push button (tactile switch) (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB cable (A to B) for programming the Arduino (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • Approximately 20 x Male-to-male jumper wires (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Laptop or desktop computer with the Arduino IDE installed (not sold by suppliers, school-provided)

How It Works

A real dice has six faces, and each face shows a pattern of dots from 1 to 6. In this project we build an "electronic dice" using 7 LEDs arranged in the same layout as the dots on a real die: one in each corner, one in the middle of each side, and one in the very centre. By turning different combinations of these 7 LEDs on or off, we can recreate any dice face using lights instead of dots.

The Arduino's job is to pick a random number between 1 and 6, just like a real dice roll, and then light up the correct pattern of LEDs for that number. We use a push button as the "roll" trigger — when a student presses it, the Arduino quickly flashes through random patterns (to look like the dice is tumbling), then settles on one final number and shows that pattern steadily.

Computers are not naturally good at true randomness — they follow instructions exactly. So we use a trick called "seeding" the random number generator: we read tiny, unpredictable electrical noise from an unused analog pin and use that number to kick off the randomness. This makes each dice roll feel genuinely unpredictable, just like a real dice.

We also use a concept called "debouncing." A mechanical button doesn't switch cleanly — it can register several rapid presses in the split second you press it, because the metal contacts bounce. We add a small delay in the code so the Arduino only counts one clean press each time.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Place the breadboard in front of you and insert the Arduino nearby, connected to the computer via USB.
  2. Insert all 7 LEDs into the breadboard, spaced out, with the longer leg (positive/anode) facing the same direction for all of them for consistency.
  3. Connect a 220 ohm resistor in series with the shorter leg (cathode) of each LED, running to the breadboard's ground rail.
  4. Connect the ground rail of the breadboard to the Arduino's GND pin using a jumper wire.
  5. Wire the longer leg (anode) side of each LED (through its resistor arrangement, or directly if resistor is on the cathode side — be consistent) to Arduino digital pins 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, one LED per pin. Arrange the LEDs physically on the breadboard to mimic a real dice face: top-left, top-right, middle-left, centre, middle-right, bottom-left, bottom-right.
  6. Insert the push button into the breadboard, straddling the centre gap so its two legs are electrically separate on each side.
  7. Connect one leg of the button to Arduino digital pin 9, and the other leg (on the opposite side of the gap) to GND.
  8. Leave the A0 analog pin unconnected — this floating pin will be used to generate random "noise" for seeding random numbers.
  9. Double-check every LED is oriented the correct way (flat edge / shorter leg to ground) before powering on.
  10. Open the Arduino IDE, paste in the provided code, select the correct board and port, and upload it.
  11. Ask students to press the button and observe: the LEDs should flicker rapidly through different dice patterns for about a second, then stop on one final number.
  12. Have students press the button multiple times and record the numbers shown, checking that all six patterns (1 through 6) appear correctly over repeated presses.
  13. If an LED patterns looks wrong (e.g. missing dot, wrong dot lit), check that pin is wired to the correct LED and that the LED is not inserted backwards.

Full Code


// Digital Dice - 7 LEDs show a random dice roll (1-6) when a button is pressed

const int numLEDs = 7;                       // We have 7 LEDs, one for each dice dot position
int ledPins[numLEDs] = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; // Pin assigned to each LED, in order:
                                              // 0=TopLeft, 1=TopRight, 2=MiddleLeft,
                                              // 3=Centre, 4=MiddleRight, 5=BottomLeft, 6=BottomRight

const int buttonPin = 9; // Push button connected here, other leg to GND

// Each row below is the LED pattern (on/off) for dice numbers 1 to 6
// Order matches ledPins array: TL, TR, ML, C, MR, BL, BR
int dicePatterns[6][numLEDs] = {
  {0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0}, // 1: just the centre dot
  {1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1}, // 2: top-left and bottom-right
  {1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1}, // 3: diagonal plus centre
  {1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1}, // 4: all four corners
  {1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1}, // 5: four corners plus centre
  {1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1}  // 6: two columns of three
};

void setup() {
  for (int i = 0; i < numLEDs; i++) {
    pinMode(ledPins[i], OUTPUT); // Set every LED pin as an output
  }
  pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT_PULLUP); // Button uses internal pull-up resistor
                                    // so pin reads HIGH normally, LOW when pressed

  randomSeed(analogRead(A0)); // Seed randomness using electrical noise on an
                              // unconnected analog pin, so rolls are unpredictable
}

void loop() {
  // Check if the button is pressed (LOW because of INPUT_PULLUP wiring)
  if (digitalRead(buttonPin) == LOW) {
    delay(20);                       // Small delay to debounce the button
    if (digitalRead(buttonPin) == LOW) { // Confirm it's still pressed after debounce
      rollDice();                    // Run the dice roll animation and result
      while (digitalRead(buttonPin) == LOW) {
        // Wait here until the student releases the button,
        // so one press doesn't trigger multiple rolls
      }
    }
  }
}

void rollDice() {
  // Step 1: Fast flashing animation to look like the dice is "tumbling"
  for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {           // Flash 15 times quickly
    int randomFace = random(0, 6);         // Pick a random index from 0 to 5
    showPattern(randomFace);               // Display that random pattern
    delay(60);                             // Short pause so it looks like flickering
  }

  // Step 2: Choose the final result and show it steadily
  int finalFace = random(0, 6);            // Pick the final dice number (index 0-5)
  showPattern(finalFace);                  // Light up the final pattern
}

void showPattern(int faceIndex) {
  // Turns on/off each LED according to the chosen dice pattern
  for (int i = 0; i < numLEDs; i++) {
    digitalWrite(ledPins[i], dicePatterns[faceIndex][i]);
  }
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
One LED never lights up, even during animationLED inserted backwards, or wired to the wrong pinCheck LED orientation (longer leg = positive) and confirm the pin number matches its position in the ledPins array
Wrong dots light up for a given number (e.g. shows an L-shape instead of a diagonal)Physical LED position on the breadboard does not match the order used in the code (TL, TR, ML, C, MR, BL, BR)Re-check the physical layout against the code comments, or relabel which pin goes to which LED position
Button press does nothing, or LEDs stay off entirelyButton wired incorrectly, or INPUT_PULLUP logic not understood (forgetting button is LOW when pressed)Confirm one leg goes to pin 9 and the other to GND, and confirm code checks for LOW, not HIGH
Same dice number shows up almost every timeMissing or incorrect randomSeed() call, or A0 pin accidentally connected to something fixedEnsure randomSeed(analogRead(A0)) is in setup() and A0 pin has no wire connected to it
One press triggers multiple rapid rollsNo debounce or no "wait for release" logicConfirm the debounce delay and the while (digitalRead(buttonPin) == LOW) loop are present and unmodified

Discussion Questions

  • Why do we need 7 LEDs instead of just displaying a number using fewer lights?
  • What would happen if we removed the randomSeed() line — do you think the "randomness" would change each time you restart the Arduino?
  • Why does the button need a pull-up resistor (or INPUT_PULLUP) instead of just connecting it directly?
  • How is a "debounce" delay similar to something that happens in real life, like a light switch or door bell?
  • Can you think of another everyday device that needs to generate a "random" outcome, like a game show wheel or slot machine? How might it work internally?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Change the flashing speed of the "rolling" animation so it looks either slower and more dramatic, or faster and more energetic.
  • Medium: Add a buzzer that makes a short beep every time the dice lands on its final number, using tone().
  • Hard: Build a second identical dice circuit (7 more LEDs and a second button, or share one button for both) so two dice roll together, and add code that adds the two results and displays the total using a 7-segment display or serial monitor output.
